deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E260 Euler models a steady pipe-flow system. An upper reservoir is kept full and feeds pipes of variable cross-section. Friction is a resistance per unit length inversely proportional to the linear size of the section (f, g, ...). Judging from the formulas on this and the next page, the resistance is proportional to α(v + l), where v is the 'height due to the velocity' and l is a constant. Integrating along a uniform segment of length x and linear size f therefore gives exponential factors e^{-αx/f}.

End of §43: the theory presupposes that inflowing water enters at the rate at which the free surface sinks. To match experiments, the upper vessel must therefore be very wide compared with the orifice (ff ≫ kk). Then pouring water in slowly does not disturb the motion, because the surface sinks very slowly.

§44: Euler's programme is to work out simple cases and compare them with experiment, so that the single friction constant α can be determined. Once α is known, any complicated system follows from the general formulas, including the loss of velocity due to friction. He sets 𝔣 = k^4/f^4 ≈ 0. Since 𝔣 = (k/f)^4, the condition f > 3k gives 𝔣 < 1/81, which he treats as negligible.

Case I (§45): a reservoir of cross-section ff and height AB = a, kept full, sits above a vertical cylindrical tube of length b and cross-section gg. The tube's bottom has an orifice kk, and 𝔣 = 0. He defines:
- 𝔄 = e^{-αa/f} and 𝔅 = e^{-αb/g}, the friction attenuation factors over the reservoir height and the tube length;
- A = (1−𝔄)/α and B = (1−𝔅)/α.

On the next page, with cos ζ = 1 (vertical tube) and 𝔤 = k^4/g^4, this gives the efflux velocity-height:
v = (A𝔅 f + B g − l(1−𝔄𝔅)) / (1 − αB𝔤).
He then expands this in powers of α to obtain frictionless-plus-correction series. The frictionless limit is v = a + b (Torricelli for total head) when 𝔤 is negligible; the first-order correction is −α(aa/2f + ab/g + bb/2g + al/f + bl/g).
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The claim f > 3k ⇒ k^4/f^4 < 1/81 is correct. Dropping 𝔣 then perturbs the velocity-height by roughly 1%, which is acceptable for comparison with 18th-century experiments.

ideas.what: The modelling assumption that a reservoir 'kept full' must be very wide, or the inflow kinetics distort the efflux. Euler resolves the paradox of §§41–43 by requiring ff ≫ kk.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli (Hydrodynamica, 1738) and earlier hydraulic tradition
ideas.where_published: E260 itself; also Euler's hydraulic memoirs of the 1750s

ideas.what: Calibration programme: determine the single friction constant α from simple experimental cases, then predict arbitrarily complicated pipe systems.
ideas.modern_name: Empirical calibration of a pipe friction coefficient (precursor of Chézy/Darcy–Weisbach practice)
ideas.where_published: E260 (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 6, 1761); discussed in Truesdell's introductions to Opera omnia ser. II vols. 12–13 (unsure of exact pages)

ideas.what: Steady flow with a friction term proportional to (velocity-height + constant) divided by the section's linear size. This yields exponential attenuation factors e^{-αa/f} and e^{-αb/g} and a closed-form efflux formula for a reservoir plus vertical tube.
ideas.modern_name: One-dimensional energy equation with quadratic (plus constant) wall resistance; head-loss with hydraulic-radius scaling

deep.surprise_reason: The page states the experimental calibration plan and sets up the first special case of Euler's frictional pipe-flow theory. This is an early quadratic-resistance pipe theory that predates Chézy, but E260 is a known published memoir and is discussed in Truesdell's historical introductions. Nothing here appears unrecorded.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. The exponents are correctly e^{-αa/f} and e^{-αb/g}. In the image, 𝔅 is followed directly by 'A = (1−𝔄)/α' without a separating semicolon. 'Huic' is correct, though the scan looks like 'Huíc'.
